newsitem.title: GREECE: DRACHMA SEEN CHARGING TOWARDS 309 AGAINST ECU.
newsitem.headline: DRACHMA SEEN CHARGING TOWARDS 309 AGAINST ECU.

text.p: The drachma is poised to test 309 support against the ecu in the near future but might spend some time in the 309.20/60 area before it resumes its climb to conquer higher ground, forex dealers said on Friday.
Ecu/drachma was trading around 309.16/21 in late dealings on Friday after opening at 309.38. It was hovering around 310.0/20 last Friday evening and 312.00/50 in late May.

"Ecu/drachma is in a downward channel and will soon test 309 support," said a chief forex dealer at a foreign bank. "It might consolidate for a while in 309.20/60 but improving fundamentals and the central bank's commitment to the hard drachma policy will prop the drachma up again."

The central bank has pre-announced it wants to keep the drachma stable against the major currencies that make up the ecu to facilitate the attainment of its final goal of bringing inflation down to 4.5 percent year-on-year at end-97 and below 3.0 percent by end-98.
Consumer price inflation was running at 5.5 percent in June.

The dealer pointed to the central bank's move to cut its two depo facility rates by 30 basis points to 11.60 percent and 9.60 percent that strengthened the drachma as proof of the credibility of the hard drachma policy.

"The market is convinced that the Bank of Greece is committed to the hard drachma policy," he said. "This explains why the drachma firmed against the ecu following the announcement of interest rate cuts on Thursday."
The drachma has been rising against the ecu since late May when sales of 2.0 billion ecus for drachmas by the Bank of Greece helped cap the ecu's advance vis-a-vis the drachma above 312.50.

Some local dealers said London-based banks devised a play in late May whereas drachmas borrowed through forex forwards in long tenors at 10.50/80 percent were placed at much higher short-term interbank rates, usually around 12 percent or higher.

The spike in short-run rates was attributed to a liquidity squeeze mainly caused by purchases of spot ecus for drachmas by the same London-based players and led to huge forex outflows in the same period.
But other dealers said a good chunk of forex outflows in late May reflected the closing out of ecu/drachma positions and blamed local players for driving long-term interest rates too low.
Some dealers said the rate cuts by the central bank that went into effect on Friday made the risk-reward profile for this type of investment play less attractive.

"The central bank's decision to cut its intervention rates lowered short-term rates and the return for investors who place their drachmas in the short end of the curve," said Angela Papageorgiou, head of money desk at Barclays Bank, Athens.
The drachma had another hiccup last week but the central bank again intervened, selling about $1.0 billion for drachmas to stem the ecu's rise against the national currency.

"Last week's move was purely speculative and it did not work out the way it was intended to," said anoher senior forex dealer. "Players who bought ecus above 310 will have to either lower their break even point or take their losses by squaring positions."
Any level below 309 could trigger stop losses on running long ecu/drachma positions that could stretch the drachma's winning streak against the ecu, the dealer said.

"You do not have much of a choice if trapped," he said. "You either buy more ecus at current levels to average down which is not prudent in my view or sell ecus for drachmas and take your losses." -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
